value.overview: The Scissor-tailed Flycatcher is a striking open-country flycatcher named for the male’s exceptionally long, forked tail. It breeds mainly in the southern Great Plains and nearby regions of the United States, where it uses grasslands, savannas, ranches, and scattered trees. Its pale gray body, salmon-pink flanks, dark wings, and distinctive tail make it one of North America’s most recognizable flycatchers. It feeds largely on flying insects captured from exposed perches.
value.classification: The Scissor-tailed Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Tyrannus. It is closely related to other large, open-country flycatchers such as the Western and Eastern kingbirds.
value.identification: Adults have a pale gray head and back, dark wings, a whitish throat, and a pale underside washed with salmon or pink, especially on the flanks and underwings. The long, deeply forked tail is most extended in adult males; females and young birds usually have shorter tails. In flight, the contrasting dark wings, pale body, and pinkish underparts are conspicuous. Its call is a series of sharp, sometimes sputtering notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds mainly from Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas northward into parts of the central United States, with smaller breeding populations farther west and east. It winters primarily in Mexico and Central America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare migrant and winter visitor rather than a regular breeding bird, with records especially from open lowlands, agricultural areas, savannas, ranches, and other disturbed habitats. It generally avoids dense mature forest.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in the United States move south after the breeding season, and some reach Costa Rica during migration or the northern winter. In Costa Rica, occurrence is localized and relatively uncommon, with sightings more likely in open habitats than in forest.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs from late spring through summer in open landscapes with scattered trees, including prairies, pastures, ranches, shelterbelts, and agricultural margins. The nest is a shallow cup made from grasses, plant fibers, and other materials, placed in a tree or shrub. Both adults defend the nesting area and care for the young. Clutch size commonly ranges from three to five eggs, and pairs may raise more than one brood where conditions are favorable.
value.dietFeeding: The Scissor-tailed Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects such as grasshoppers, beetles, wasps, bees, and moths. It usually hunts from an exposed perch, launching into the air to seize prey before returning to the same or another perch. It may also take insects from vegetation or the ground and occasionally eats berries and other small fruits, especially outside the breeding season.
value.behavior: This species is conspicuous, active, and strongly territorial during the breeding season. Adults often perform graceful aerial chases and tail-displaying flights while defending territories or communicating with mates. They commonly perch on fences, utility wires, dead branches, and isolated shrubs. Outside the breeding season they are less territorial and may gather loosely in suitable open habitats. Their long tail does not prevent agile flight and may be used in display.

conservation.populationTrend: Available broad-scale monitoring indicates a long-term decline in parts of its range, although the species is still locally common in suitable breeding habitat and remains globally widespread.
conservation.threats: Habitat conversion and degradation in open-country breeding areas, including intensive agriculture, removal of scattered trees, and loss of native grasslands, may reduce nesting and foraging opportunities. Pesticide use can also reduce insect prey. In Costa Rica, the main concern is the continued loss or alteration of open lowland habitats used by migrants and wintering birds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native grasslands, savannas, pastures, and agricultural landscapes with scattered mature trees and shrubs. Reduce unnecessary insecticide use, maintain hedgerows and natural field edges, and preserve wetlands and other productive open habitats along migration routes. In Costa Rica, reporting sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can help clarify the species’ uncommon distribution and seasonal status.
